tagline.text: An 84-tier waterfall cascading through the Mindanao rainforest

image.credit: Andre Lloyd Torres / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Andrew Gil Desabelle / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A tiered waterfall in the rainforest of Cateel, Davao Oriental, cascading about 340m down more than 80 rock steps. It sits right beside the road, so it's easy to reach, and you can swim in jade-colored pools and ride a zipline across the falls.
Aliwagwag Falls is a tiered waterfall in the mountain village of Aliwagwag in Cateel, Davao Oriental, at the eastern tip of Mindanao. The falls total about
(roughly 1,110 feet) in height, made up of a series of about
84 tiers

, each 2–34m tall, and are often introduced as one of the tallest waterfalls in the Philippines. White water tumbles down the limestone steps layer by layer, pooling into jade-colored basins below, in a scene that looks like a giant staircase of water.
The area around the falls was designated the roughly 10,000-hectare Aliwagwag Protected Landscape by presidential proclamation in
, and its protected status was further strengthened by law in

. This forest, home to the headwaters of the Cateel River, is one of the largest remaining stretches of lowland rainforest in Mindanao, sheltering the Philippine eagle and several endemic birds, as well as the toog tree, known as the tallest tree species in the Philippines.

The falls sit right beside the mountain road linking Compostela, Davao de Oro, and Cateel, so a huge advantage is that you can see them the moment you step out of the car, without a long trek. The province-run Aliwagwag Falls Eco Park has a tiered viewing walkway, viewpoints, picnic huts, showers, and a zipline crossing above the falls. In
December 2012
, Typhoon Pablo (Bopha) battered the Cateel area severely, but the forest and falls have since recovered.
Because it's a remote spot, about
4–5 hours

one-way from downtown Davao, foreign travelers are still rare here, and weekends mainly draw local families on outings. It's worth recommending to travelers who want to see a large waterfall that's still relatively untouched, or anyone continuing their trip along Mindanao's eastern coast.

From the eco park entrance, climb the steps and walkway beside the falls to see one tier after another. Try to capture the whole falls once from the wide pool below and once from the midway viewpoint.
The shallow, wide pool below the falls has clear, cold water, good for cooling off on a hot day. Swim only where staff permit, and stay away from tiers with a strong current.

Riding the zipline across the falls' valley lets you look down over the 84-tier falls and forest from the air. Whether it's running and its price change with the weather and maintenance schedule, so check on-site.

blocks.title: The view from the roadside overlook

children.text: From the curves and bridge along the Compostela–Cateel road, the whole falls come into view at once. Photos are best when the morning sun catches the water.
Cross the hanging bridge (monkey bridge) over the valley around the falls to feel the sound and spray of the water up close. The planks get slippery after rain, so cross slowly.
The mountain road from Compostela to the falls winds past primeval forest and valleys, making for a scenic drive. On a clear day, the layered mountain ridges outside the window are striking.

blocks.title: Exploring the coastal town of Cateel

children.text: Head down from the falls to reach the town and beach of Cateel, facing the Pacific. It's a good way to end the day with quiet fishing-village scenery and fresh seafood.

Direct flights from Manila to Francisco Bangoy International Airport, Davao (DVO) take about
1 hour 50 minutes
, with one-way fares around
. From the airport, it's about
30–40 minutes
by taxi to the Davao City Overland Transport Terminal (DCOTT) in Ecoland.
Taking a bus or van from DCOTT bound for Cateel
via Compostela
takes about
4–5 hours
, for around
. This route passes right by the falls, so tell the driver in advance to let you off at Aliwagwag Falls Eco Park.
Even though it's also bound for Cateel, the coastal route via Mati takes about
7–9 hours
, so be sure to confirm the route when buying your ticket. The first bus often leaves before dawn and departures aren't frequent, so it's best to check the schedule at the terminal the day before.
From Davao, go through Panabo–Tagum to Compostela, then it's about
4–5 hours
on the Compostela–Cateel mountain road. If you're in a group, chartering a van with driver (about
for 2 days, 1 night) is the most convenient option.
The mountain stretch past Compostela has many sharp curves and climbs, and heavy rain can delay travel with rockfalls and landslides. Always travel during daylight.
It's about
30–45 minutes
from the falls to Cateel town, traveled by chartered habal-habal (motorbike taxi) or tricycle. One-way fares run around
, depending on the number of passengers and negotiation.
Flag down a return bus on the road in front of the falls. Seats can fill up late in the afternoon, so head out early.
Cateel sits on Mindanao's east coast facing the Pacific, so
November–February

, when the northeast monsoon (Amihan) blows, brings the heaviest rain. The falls swell dramatically at this time, but the water turns muddy and the current too strong for swimming, and the mountain road faces a higher risk of rockfalls and landslides.
March–September
, with relatively less rain, offers clearer water and easier travel, making it the best time to visit.
Midday temperatures run around
, but the forest around the falls is noticeably cooler and the water quite cold. Davao Oriental sits somewhat outside the main typhoon path, but a strong typhoon occasionally passes through around
December
, so check the forecast. Holy Week and school-break weekends in
April–May
draw large crowds of local visitors, so choose a weekday morning if you want a quieter visit.

Inside the eco park is a simple province-run traveler's lodge, with fan rooms running about
a night and air-conditioned rooms around

, plus group rooms for several people. The biggest advantage is falling asleep to the sound of the falls and seeing them empty early in the morning. For more options, use a guesthouse or small hotel in Cateel town (about
). Most facilities are simple, so it's best to keep your expectations modest.

In front of the eco park are small restaurants and stalls selling rice and side dishes, but the menu is limited and some close early. Renting a picnic hut and bringing your own packed meal or grilling ingredients is the local way to enjoy the place. In Cateel town, you can cheaply try coastal dishes such as grilled fish caught in the Pacific, kinilaw (raw fish cured in vinegar), and ginataan (dishes simmered in coconut milk).
Only the route via Compostela passes the falls. Boarding the wrong bus via Mati by mistake will nearly double your travel time.
The eco park is generally open from
8 AM to 5 PM
. A day trip from Davao is impractical, so an overnight stay near the falls is recommended.
Cell signal is weak or drops out around the falls and along parts of the mountain road. Save your accommodation's and transport contacts, and an offline map, in advance.
ATMs can be scarce even in Cateel town. Bring plenty of cash from Davao to cover your needs.
The rock steps are very slippery with moss. Wear aqua shoes or sandals with non-slip soles.
If you want clear water, it's best to avoid the day right after rain. The water clears up again quickly, often after just a day or two without rain.
For drone footage or group events, check with the eco park office first. There may be rules in place since this is a protected area.

Security conditions in the mountainous areas of Davao Oriental and Davao de Oro change from time to time. Before you go, check your home country's latest travel advisories and notices from the local tourism office, and never travel the mountain road after dark.
The eco-park closed temporarily for safety inspections after the magnitude 7.4 earthquake off Davao Oriental on
October 10, 2025
, and the provincial government finished its on-site inspection in
February 2026

and is preparing to reopen. Before departure, be sure to check with the Cateel tourism office or the eco-park's Facebook page whether it is open and whether the zip line and suspension bridge are operating.
After heavy rain, the falls swell rapidly and the current turns strong. Never enter the water if it's muddy or if staff restrict access.
The Compostela–Cateel road can be blocked by rockfalls and landslides during the rainy season. Check road conditions before you set out.
The upper tiers of the falls are very dangerous if you stray off the walkway. Don't stand at the edge of wet rocks for a photo.
Within the protected area, carry out all your trash, and don't collect plants or rocks.
The forest around the falls may have mosquitoes and leeches. Bring insect repellent and long clothing.
